title: Outcomes against who lives nearby, tract by tract
question: Are projects more often refused, changed or put off in census tracts with lower incomes, more renters or a different mix of residents, once like cases are compared?
finding: Of 1,718 decisions placed in a census tract, 46.2% of 517 in the lowest-income third of tracts went against the project or were continued (44.6% expected from the mix of cases) and 49.4% of 644 in the highest-income third (50.1% expected). The neighborhood-level link in the planning-applications screen (non-approval lower where incomes are higher, -0.52) points the same way but is within what chance would produce at tract level, and on no Census measure do the lowest and highest thirds differ, like for like, by more than chance would produce.
how: Every commission action on a project at an address (2019-2022), every Board of Appeals case on a building permit appealed by someone other than the holder (September 2022 to November 2026) and every decided Board of Supervisors appeal against an approval (2015-2026) is placed in a 2020 census tract through the City’s address file or the parcel. “Against the project” means: at the commissions, disapproved, changed after discretionary review, or continued; at the Board of Appeals, the permit conditioned or overturned; at the Board of Supervisors, the appeal upheld. Tracts are ranked by each Census measure (2020-24 five-year estimates) and cut into thirds with equal numbers of tracts; “expected” gives every case the citywide rate for its body and kind. The rank correlation uses only tracts with 20 or more cases and is called beyond chance at about the 1-in-100 level. Tracts with under 500 residents are left out.
limits: AREA LEVEL ONLY: these are Census figures for tracts and say nothing about any applicant, neighbor or appellant. A tract with many cases may be a commercial area whose residents are few and unlike the people who own, build or object there. Three bodies, three periods and three meanings of “against” are pooled, so the pooled rate is a rough index. Tracts differ in what is proposed: review requests, for example, are concentrated in higher-income tracts (next table), and a continuance may be asked for by the applicant. Survey margins are wide for single tracts, and only a handful of tracts have 20 cases. A difference between areas, or between groups of cases, is not proof of bias. Areas differ in what is proposed, in zoning, lot sizes, building ages and land prices, and in who chooses to apply, object or appeal at all.
